message.content:
You are joining a reverse-engineering project. First read /tmp/notes/ARCH.md completely — it explains the task, the strict rules (black-box only: never decompile/trace/read the original binary, never use `executable serve`; no internet), the repo layout, and the comparison tools in /tmp/agent-tools/.

Your job: the sketch pen and the drawing/stack layouts — byte-identical to the original.
1. `|sketch|` (prim Sketch) and its derivatives `|hidden|`, `|wall|`/`|partition|` geometry only: the `draw:` pen language — move(x,y), up/down/left/right(n), line(dx,dy), angle(deg, n) (0 = up, clockwise), arc(...) in its forms (tangent `arc(r, sweep)`, two-point `arc(dx, dy, r)`, three-number forms…), curve(c1x, c1y, c2x, c2y, x, y), circle(r), chamfer(n), fillet(n), point(), close(), multiple subpaths, segment tags `right(8):head` (used later by dimensions as anchors — keep the tagged segments accessible on the node), `fill-rule="evenodd"` output, `mirror: x-axis|y-axis` (an open subpath fuses across the axis and generates an axis `|centerline|`; a closed one is duplicated), `pattern: grid(nx, ny, dx, dy)` / `radial(n, r)` (copies of a feature; radial generates a `|pitch-circle|`), `revolve: x-axis` (turned part: half profile → whole, plus axis + edge lines), `break:` (break gap in a long part), `thread:` (threaded run rendering). Holes (`|hole|`, an oval with generated centre-line chrome `|line| { chrome: x-axis/y-axis }`), `|centerline|`, `|pitch-circle|`, `|plane|`(geometry only if simple).
2. `layout: stack` (all children share one datum/origin — e.g. assets/test_samples/logo.lini, test_doc_examples/skill_06.lini, spec_30.lini) and `layout: drawing` / `|drawing|` blocks (unit mm, density (px per unit, default 4), `scale:` ratio, `px-per-unit`, how parts are placed on the drawing's origin, drawing padding, how the drawing participates in the outer flow). `layout: floorplan` is a dialect of drawing (unit m, scale 0.02 etc.) — handle its unit/scale maths if it falls out naturally, but floor-plan furniture/walls/doors are NOT your job.
Not your job (another wave): dimension/leader/datum/feature-control annotations (`(-)`, `(o)`, `<-`, `*-`, `>-`, `||` statements, `|feature-control|`, `|datum|`, `|surface-finish|`, `|balloon|`, `|title-block|`, `|page|`), charts, links. If a test file contains annotations, it's fine for it to still fail — focus on getting the geometry/parts byte-identical (compare the relevant lines).

Hooks: add a branch in `layout::measure` and `render::render_node` (and a module e.g. `src/sketch.rs`, `src/drawing.rs`); keep edits to shared files minimal and additive. `desugar` output (`executable desugar FILE`) is a great window into how these lower (e.g. holes gain `|line| .lini-centerline.lini-line { chrome: x-axis; }` children, drawings get `px-per-unit: 4`) — use it to understand the model. Type defaults already in src/types.rs (sketch, hidden, hole, centerline, pitch-circle, plane, drawing, stack…).

Test files: test_doc_examples prop_draw, prop_mirror, prop_revolve, prop_break, prop_density, prop_pattern, prop_thread, skill_06, skill_07 (geometry part), spec_28, spec_30, spec_42 (geometry), blocks equivalents; test_samples logo.lini, sketch.lini, drawing_turned.lini (geometry), drawing_section.lini (geometry). Write many synthetic snippets in /tmp/<you>/ to pin down each pen command's exact path output and number formatting (note some paths may print raw f64 Display rather than the 4-decimal format — check).

Before committing, run the full asset comparison (`cmpw.py /tmp/bin-sketch/executable assets/test_doc_examples/*.lini assets/test_samples/*.lini`) and ensure nothing that passed before regresses (starting count: 71/209). Commit on your branch and report: pass counts, implemented features, shared-file edits, known gaps, and notes useful for whoever implements drawing annotations next (how tagged segments/anchors are stored, units/scale).

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git

- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).

# Lini reimplementation — notes for contributors

## The task (read carefully)
We are reimplementing, from scratch in Rust (std only, no crates), a closed binary at
`/workspace/executable` ("lini 1.1.0", a diagram compiler: Lini source → SVG). Our build must
produce byte-identical stdout/stderr/exit codes for every input. Hidden tests compare outputs
exactly, so a test only passes when the whole output matches.

RULES (strict):
- Learn behaviour ONLY by running `/workspace/executable` with inputs and reading its output.
  NEVER decompile/disassemble it, never use strace/ltrace/gdb on it, never read its bytes.
- No internet, no looking for lini source code anywhere. std-only Rust.
- Do not run `./compile.sh` in /workspace (it would try to overwrite the original binary).
- Keep scratch scripts OUTSIDE the repo (e.g. /tmp/<you>/). Non-Rust code in the repo is limited.

- Do NOT use `executable serve` or anything it serves over HTTP. Stick to the CLI
  (compile, --json, --static, --embed-font, desugar, fmt, highlight, theme) as your oracle.

## Docs / samples
- `/workspace/README.md` (overview), `/workspace/assets/` — sample inputs:
  `test_doc_examples/*.lini` (one per documented property, plus SPEC/SKILL snippets),
  `test_samples/*.lini` (larger feature boards), `test_images/mark.png`.
  The hidden test-suite is very likely more files of the same kinds.

## Build & compare
- In your checkout: `cargo build --release` → `target/release/lini`.
- Copy it to a private dir under the name `executable` (help/usage text uses argv[0]):
  `mkdir -p /tmp/bin-<you> && cp target/release/lini /tmp/bin-<you>/executable`
- Tools in `/tmp/agent-tools/` (shared, read-only use):
  - `cmpw.py /tmp/bin-<you>/executable [-a "args"] files...` → OK n / m and failing files.
  - `dw /tmp/bin-<you>/executable file.lini [args]` → diff (original vs ours).
  - `rr 'lini source' [args]` → run the ORIGINAL on a snippet (prints output + [exit N]).
  - `rm2 /tmp/bin-<you>/executable 'lini source' [args]` → diff on a snippet.
- Font metric helper (python, for exploration): `/tmp/scripts/tw.py` / `/tmp/scripts/ttf.py`.

## Code map (src/)
- `main.rs` — CLI dispatch (`cli.rs` emulates clap), `compile_src()` pipeline:
  parse → `scene::build_sheet` → `scene::Builder` (node tree) → `compile::compute` (cascade +
  `Computed` per node) → `layout::measure(ctx, 0, None)` → `render::render`.
- `lexer.rs`, `parser.rs`, `ast.rs` — tokens / recursive descent / syntax tree. Errors are
  fail-fast: first `Diag` aborts (`diag.rs` has codes & text/JSON rendering).
- `scene.rs` — `SheetModel` (root config decls, vars, bindings, type rules, defines, classes,
  id rules, link rules), `Node` (prim, `chain` = type chain most-derived first, id, classes,
  inline decls, text, children, `props` = cascaded decls map, layout fields w/h = rect size,
  x/y = centre relative to parent centre), `Builder` (statements → nodes).
- `types.rs` — built-in type registry (name, primitive, base, defaults as lini decl text).
- `style.rs` — value helpers (`value_num(s)`, `ident_of`, colour/weight/dash serialisation).
- `compile.rs` — `Ctx` (all state), `cascade()` (type chain base-first: defaults then user
  `|type|` rules; then classes; id rules; inline), `compute()` fills `ctx.comp[i]: Computed`
  (font size/weight/family, padding, gap, direction, align, justify, width/height, stroke…).
- `layout.rs` — `measure()` dispatch (text, line/poly/path geometry, chart hook, grid, flow).
  `outer(ctx,i)` = rect size + stroke width when stroke != none (text: its box).
- `render.rs` — SVG + stylesheet. CSS rules are collected as (slot, text) and sorted by
  `SLOT_ORDER`; families push extra rules into `out.extra_rules`. Root `--lini-*` vars are
  emitted for every var referenced (`use_var(&mut out.vars, name)`), sorted by name.
  The scope class is `lini-scope-` + hash8(style text written with `.lini` as scope).
- `util.rs` — `f4()` (all coordinates: `{:.4}` then trim zeros; "-0"→"0"), `hash8()` (FNV-1a 64,
  folded hi^lo, 8 hex), `xml_escape`, `base64`, `levenshtein`.
- `font.rs` — bundled TTFs (extracted via `--embed-font`); `text_width(family, weight, size, s)`.
- `markers.rs` — arrow/dot/diamond line-end markers. `geom.rs` — SVG path bbox.

## Facts learned so far (all verified against the original)
- Text box: width = Σ advances·size/1000 (+ letter-spacing·(n−1)); height = size for one line,
  n·1.2·size + (n−1)·line-spacing for n lines. Text renders `<text class="lini-text" x y
  dy="0.358em">`; multi-line uses tspans (first y = centre − (n−1)·pitch/2 + 0.358·size).
- Inline `style="…"` on a node = its own/inline decls minus those equal to what its CSS rules
  (type chain + classes) already give, in CSS_ORDER.
- Indentation: 2 spaces per nesting level; scene children start at 4.
- Only the first error is reported (`file:line:col: error: msg`, exit 1); warnings are printed
  before the SVG and do not change exit code (unless --strict).

## Links (already in place)
- `scene::Builder::resolve_links()` resolves every link statement after the node tree is built:
  ids are scoped (a node with an id opens a scope for its descendants; anonymous containers are
  transparent), bare unknown names auto-create `|box#name| "name"` appended to the container,
  dotted paths resolve scope by scope, chains/fans expand in statement order (cartesian, `from`
  outer). Result: `ctx.links: Vec<scene::Link>` (from/to node indices, op string like "->",
  "-->", "<->", "~>", "-o<", "(-)", "(o)", "<-", "||" …, label, labels block, classes, style decls,
  from/to anchors (`a:right`), pattern index (`p.2`), the container node, the statement span).
  Rendering of links is NOT implemented yet (`<g class="lini-links"/>` is always empty).
- `subcommands`: fmt (src/format*), highlight (src/highlight.rs) are DONE and verified — don't touch.

## Working rules
- Put your feature in its own module(s); keep edits to shared files (main.rs, layout.rs,

systemPrompt:
You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: cmpw.py BIN [-a "extra args"] [-s N] files...
# Runs the original (/workspace/executable) and BIN on each file (cwd = file's dir),
# compares stdout, stderr and exit code. BIN must be named 'executable' (help text uses argv[0]).
import subprocess,sys,os
mine=sys.argv[1]; args=[]; files=[]; show=0
i=2
while i<len(sys.argv):
    a=sys.argv[i]
    if a=='-a': args=sys.argv[i+1].split(); i+=2; continue
    if a=='-s': show=int(sys.argv[i+1]); i+=2; continue
    files.append(a); i+=1
ORIG='/workspace/executable'
ok=0; bad=[]
for f in files:
    d=os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(f)); b=os.path.basename(f)
    r1=subprocess.run([ORIG]+args+[b],capture_output=True,cwd=d)
    try: r2=subprocess.run([mine]+args+[b],capture_output=True,cwd=d,timeout=30)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired: bad.append((f,'TIMEOUT')); continue
    if r1.stdout==r2.stdout and r1.stderr==r2.stderr and r1.returncode==r2.returncode: ok+=1
    else:
        why=[]
        if r1.returncode!=r2.returncode: why.append('exit %d/%d'%(r1.returncode,r2.returncode))
        if r1.stdout!=r2.stdout: why.append('stdout')
        if r1.stderr!=r2.stderr: why.append('stderr')
        bad.append((f,' '.join(why)))
print('OK %d / %d'%(ok,len(files)))
for f,w in (bad[:show] if show else bad): print('  FAIL',f,w)
#!/bin/bash
# usage: dw BIN file.lini [extra args]  -> diff of original vs BIN output (stderr, then stdout)
mine="$1"; f="$2"; shift 2
dir=$(dirname "$f"); b=$(basename "$f")
cd "$dir"
/workspace/executable "$@" "$b" > /tmp/dw_o.$$ 2>/tmp/dw_oe.$$; e1=$?
"$mine" "$@" "$b" > /tmp/dw_m.$$ 2>/tmp/dw_me.$$; e2=$?
echo "exit $e1 / $e2"
diff /tmp/dw_oe.$$ /tmp/dw_me.$$ | head -10
diff /tmp/dw_o.$$ /tmp/dw_m.$$ | head -${DL:-60}
rm -f /tmp/dw_*.$$
#!/bin/bash
# usage: rr 'lini source' [extra args] -> runs the ORIGINAL on the snippet (file r_in.lini in a private tmp dir)
src="$1"; shift
d=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rr.XXXXXX); printf '%s' "$src" > $d/r_in.lini
cd $d && /workspace/executable "$@" r_in.lini; echo "[exit $?]"; rm -rf $d
#!/bin/bash
# usage: rm2 BIN 'lini source' [extra args] -> diff original vs BIN on a snippet
mine="$1"; src="$2"; shift 2
d=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rm2.XXXXXX); printf '%s' "$src" > $d/r_in.lini
cd $d; /workspace/executable "$@" r_in.lini > o1 2>&1; e1=$?; "$mine" "$@" r_in.lini > o2 2>&1; e2=$?
echo "exit $e1 / $e2"; diff o1 o2 | head -${DL:-60}; rm -rf $d

From mindmap to blueprint.

One small language for every kind of figure — pretty by default, precise when it has to be.

lini.rs — the tour, the reference, the gallery, and the compiler in your browser

Thirty-odd lines of Lini — samples/hero.lini.

--- ## What it is A compiler: plain text in, clean themeable SVG out. You say where things go, and the parts you'd rather not do by hand — routing a wire through the gaps, measuring a dimension, picking a palette — are done for you. - **One grammar, every family.** Flowcharts, mindmaps, org charts, tables, ER schemas, sequences, charts, engineering drawings, floor plans, and circuit schematics are all layouts over the same nodes and links. Not ten tools with ten syntaxes — one language, so theming, baking, and diffing work identically in each. - **Themeable after export.** Every colour is a live CSS variable and a `light-dark()` pair, so one SVG follows the viewer's OS with no script and no re-render, and one line of host CSS recolours every diagram on a page. - **Fast and deterministic.** A typical figure compiles in about 2 ms, byte-identical every run, so SVGs diff cleanly in CI. - **No runtime.** A single native binary. No Node, no headless browser, nothing to stand up beside it. - **Agents can write it.** [`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SKILL.md) is the whole language as a working brief, and the property schema is generated from the compiler's own ledger. ## Gallery
Charts
 ER schemas
Sequence diagrams
 Icons & signs
Circuit schematics
 Engineering drawings
Floor plans
 Mindmaps & trees
More, with their source, at [lini.rs/gallery](https://lini.rs/gallery/). ## Colour

One file, both modes — samples/palette.lini.

Eleven named hues — `red rose orange amber lime green teal sky blue purple gray` — each in five **job-named** tiers: `wash` for backgrounds, `soft`, the bare name, `deep` for strokes, `ink` for text. The names hold across the flip — `--teal-ink` is the high-contrast tone in *both* modes, where a `light`/`dark` name would invert — which is what lets one export serve both. OKLCH underneath, so every ramp is perceptually even, and `gradient(--rose, --sky)` blends any two at a flattering angle. ## Install ```bash cargo install lini ``` ```bash lini diagram.lini -o diagram.svg # compile to SVG lini serve diagram.lini # live-reloading preview lini serve samples/ # browse and edit the bundled examples ``` Six lines — a type define, a container, and two links Lini routes for you: ``` { |svc::box| { fill: --teal-wash; stroke: --teal-ink } } |group| "Services" [ |svc#api| "API"; |svc#auth| "Auth" ] |svc#db| "Postgres" api -> db "read" auth -> db "write" ``` `{ }` is style, `[ ]` is children, and naming two nodes draws an orthogonal path between them, clear of everything in the way. The rest of the grammar is the [tour](https://lini.rs/docs/tour/language.html). ## Use it in your project - **[mdbook-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/mdbook-lini)** — ` ```lini ` fences in an mdBook, compiled to inline SVG at build time. On [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/mdbook-lini). - **[rehype-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/rehype-lini)** — the same fences anywhere [rehype](https://github.com/rehypejs/rehype) runs: Docusaurus, Next and MDX, or a bare `unified()` pipeline. A toggle reveals the source that drew each figure. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rehype-lini): `npm install rehype-lini`. - **[astro-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/astro-lini)** — the Astro integration: one line in `astro.config.mjs` and every fence in the site draws. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/astro-lini): `npm install astro-lini`. - **[remark-lini](https://github.com/monfa-red/remark-lini)** — the engine both of those run on, and the remark plugin for a pipeline that needs the figures drawn before a highlighter sees them. On [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/remark-lini-lang) as `remark-lini-lang`, since npm refuses the short name as one edit from `remark-lint`. - **[lini-wasm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/lini-wasm)** — the compiler itself, for JavaScript. One package, two builds, so it runs in Node, Bun, Deno, a bundler or a browser. This is what the integrations above ride on, and what to reach for to build one of your own. - **Editors** — search *Lini* in the extensions pane: a TextMate bundle on the [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=monfa-red.lini) and a tree-sitter extension in [Zed's registry](https://zed.dev/extensions?query=lini). Source for both under [`editors/`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/tree/main/editors). Their word lists are generated from the compiler's own tables, so a new property highlights the day it lands. - **As a library** — `lini` is a crate as well as a binary: [docs.rs/lini](https://docs.rs/lini). ### From the community Built and maintained by their own authors, on their own release schedules. - **[obsidian-lini-view](https://github.com/FoxMaint/obsidian-lini-view)** — the Obsidian plugin: a ` ```lini ` fence draws in the note itself, live in the editor, on `lini-wasm`. ## For agents - **[`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SKILL.md)** — the language as a working brief: the write → compile → *look at the render* loop, every family, and the mistakes worth not making. Also served at [lini.rs/SKILL.md](https://lini.rs/SKILL.md). - **[`schema/lini.schema.json`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/schema/lini.schema.json)** — every primitive, template, role, and property with its owner, value shape, resolved default, inheritance channel, and a compiled example. Generated from the same ledger the compiler reads, and CI fails on drift. [`schema/reference.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/schema/reference.md) is the compact human mirror. - **`lini --json`** — diagnostics as JSON: stable codes, spans, and machine-applicable fixes. ## Go deeper - [The tour](https://lini.rs/docs/tour/language.html) — fourteen pages, start to finish. - [The reference](https://lini.rs/docs/reference/00-at-a-glance.html) — every property, split out of the spec. - [The gallery](https://lini.rs/gallery/) — finished figures, with the source that drew them. - [The playground](https://lini.rs/play/) — the compiler, compiled to wasm, in your browser. In this repo: [`SPEC.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/SPEC.md) is the language contract, frozen for 1.x — syntax, property names, defaults, diagnostic codes, and the theming surface stay compatible. [`ROUTING.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/ROUTING.md) is the routing contract. [`samples/`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/tree/main/samples) holds one file per feature area, and [`RELEASING.md`](https://github.com/monfa-red/lini/blob/main/RELEASING.md) says how the pieces #!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: m.py [-f] [-a "args"] [-g REGEX] [-b BIN] 'snippet' ...   (or -t TEMPLATE with {} and values)
# Runs the ORIGINAL (or BIN) on each snippet and prints filtered output lines.
import subprocess, sys, os, tempfile, re
args = sys.argv[1:]
extra = []; grep = r'path|error|warning|<line|polyline|ellipse|<rect|translate|viewBox|<circle|<polygon'
full = False; tmpl = None; binp = '/workspace/executable'
snips = []
i = 0
while i < len(args):
    a = args[i]
    if a == '-a': extra = args[i+1].split(); i += 2; continue
    if a == '-g': grep = args[i+1]; i += 2; continue
    if a == '-f': full = True; i += 1; continue
    if a == '-b': binp = args[i+1]; i += 2; continue
    if a == '-t': tmpl = args[i+1]; i += 2; continue
    snips.append(a); i += 1
if tmpl is not None:
    snips = [tmpl.replace('{}', v) for v in snips]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='m_')
for s in snips:
    p = os.path.join(d, 'r_in.lini')
    open(p, 'w').write(s)
    r = subprocess.run([binp] + extra + ['r_in.lini'], capture_output=True, cwd=d)
    out = r.stdout.decode() + r.stderr.decode()
    print('###', s.replace('\n', '\\n')[:200])
    for line in out.split('\n'):
        if full:
            if re.search(r'^    \.lini|^      :root|^      \.lini|^    @layer|^    }|<style>|</style>|lini-links|^</svg>', line):
                continue
            print(line)
        elif re.search(grep, line):
            print(line)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print('[exit %d]' % r.returncode)

import math
def arc_center(x1,y1,rx,large,sweep,x2,y2):
    dx=(x1-x2)/2; dy=(y1-y2)/2
    x1p=dx; y1p=dy
    lam=(x1p*x1p+y1p*y1p)/(rx*rx)
    if lam>1: rx*=math.sqrt(lam)
    num=rx*rx*rx*rx - rx*rx*y1p*y1p - rx*rx*x1p*x1p
    den=rx*rx*y1p*y1p + rx*rx*x1p*x1p
    co=math.sqrt(max(num/den,0))
    if large==sweep: co=-co
    cxp=co*y1p; cyp=-co*x1p
    return cxp+(x1+x2)/2, cyp+(y1+y2)/2, rx
print(arc_center(117.58,-88,12,0,0,107.501,-69.487))
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: strip.py files... -> writes copies without link/annotation statements to /tmp/sk/strip/, prints paths
import sys, os, re, shutil
out = '/tmp/sk/strip'
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
pat = re.compile(r'(\(-\)|\(o\)|<-|\*-|>-|\|\||->|-->|<->|~>)')
for f in sys.argv[1:]:
    lines = open(f).read().split('\n')
    keep = []
    skip_block = 0
    for l in lines:
        code = l.split('//')[0]
        if skip_block:
            skip_block += code.count('[') - code.count(']')
            continue
        if pat.search(code) and not code.strip().startswith('|') and '"' not in code.split(pat.search(code).group(0))[0]:
            # a link statement; swallow a trailing [ ... ] block
            depth = code.count('[') - code.count(']')
            if depth > 0:
                skip_block = depth
            continue
        keep.append(l)
    p = os.path.join(out, os.path.basename(f))
    open(p, 'w').write('\n'.join(keep))
    print(p)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: cmp_snips.py FILE [-v] [-a args]  -> FILE holds snippets separated by lines '---'
# compares original vs /tmp/bin-sketch/executable on each, prints mismatches (diff)
import subprocess, sys, os, tempfile, difflib
args = sys.argv[1:]
verbose = '-v' in args
extra = []
if '-a' in args:
    k = args.index('-a'); extra = args[k+1].split(); del args[k:k+2]
args = [a for a in args if a != '-v']
src = open(args[0]).read()
snips = [s.strip('\n') for s in src.split('\n---\n') if s.strip()]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cs_')
ok = 0
for s in snips:
    p = os.path.join(d, 'r_in.lini')
    open(p, 'w').write(s + '\n')
    r1 = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable'] + extra + ['r_in.lini'], capture_output=True, cwd=d)
    r2 = subprocess.run(['/tmp/bin-sketch/executable'] + extra + ['r_in.lini'], capture_output=True, cwd=d)
    o1 = (r1.stderr.decode() + r1.stdout.decode() + '[exit %d]' % r1.returncode).split('\n')
    o2 = (r2.stderr.decode() + r2.stdout.decode() + '[exit %d]' % r2.returncode).split('\n')
    if o1 == o2:
        ok += 1
        continue
    print('### MISMATCH:', s.replace('\n', '\\n')[:300])
    diff = list(difflib.unified_diff(o1, o2, 'orig', 'mine', n=0, lineterm=''))
    lim = 400 if verbose else 14
    for line in diff[2:2+lim]:
        if line.startswith(('-    .lini-scope', '+    .lini-scope', '-      :root', '+      :root', '-      .lini-scope', '+      .lini-scope')) and not verbose:
            continue
        print('   ', line[:300])
print('OK %d / %d' % (ok, len(snips)))

 'curve arity': 'move(0,0) curve(1,2,3,4,5)',

 'corner arity': 'move(0,0) right(5) chamfer() down(5)',

 'corner no next': 'move(0,0) right(5) chamfer(2)',
 'corner no turn': 'move(0,0) right(5) chamfer(2) right(5)',
 'corner curve': 'move(0,0) right(10) chamfer(2) curve(0, 5, 5, 10, 10, 10)',
 'chamfer fit': 'move(0,0) right(5) chamfer(9) down(5)',
 'fillet fit': 'move(0,0) right(5) fillet(9) down(5)',
 'point args': 'move(0,0) point(1)',
 'point tag': 'move(0,0) right(5) point() down(5)',
 'close none': 'move(0,0) close()',
 'after close': 'move(0,0) right(5) close() right(3)',
 'start move': 'right(5)',

 'dup tag': 'move(0,0) right(5):a down(5):a',
 'builtin tag': 'move(0,0) right(5):left down(5)',

}
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for name, draw in cases.items():
    src = '|box| "x"\n|sketch| { draw: %s; }\n' % draw
    open(os.path.join(d, 'r_in.lini'), 'w').write(src)

    for b in ['/workspace/executable', '/tmp/bin-sketch/executable']:

    flag = 'OK ' if out[0] == out[1] else 'BAD'
    print(flag, name, out[0], '' if out[0] == out[1] else out[1])

content.text:
I've committed the sketch pen, the stack and drawing layouts, holes, patterns, revolve/break/thread chrome and section planes on `worktree-agent-ae6eb5419dc83b090` (head `29b0714`). The asset comparison is now **85/209** (from 71), with no regressions: every file that passed before still passes. The `blocks/` set is 7/37 (from 4).

**Status of the target files**
- **Pass:** prop_draw, prop_mirror, prop_revolve, prop_break, prop_density, prop_pattern, prop_thread, prop_thickness, prop_facing, skill_06, spec_28, spec_30, logo, sketch.
- **skill_07 and spec_42** fail only because of their annotation statements (`(-)`, `(o)`, `<-`). With those lines removed, the output matches the original byte for byte.
- **drawing_turned** still has annotations, plus one gap of mine (descendant selector, below); its other geometry matches.
- **drawing_section** stops with an error on `hatch()`; it also needs `|page|`, `of:` views and annotations, which aren't mine.

**What's implemented**
- **Pen (`src/sketch.rs`):** every `draw:` command. Path numbers round to 3 decimals, and bounds come from the rounded path with each arc sampled at 24 points, which is how the original does it. All the pen error messages, spans and checking order match the original.
- **Mirror:** an open subpath fuses across the axis, a closed one is duplicated. `x-axis`, `y-axis`, bearings and chained mirrors all work. Child features are reflected too (they become a wrapper holding the copies).
- **Revolve, break, thread:** shoulder lines, the axis centreline, thread lines and thread-end lines. Break cuts out the middle (12 px gap), draws the zigzag break lines, and slides or folds children that sit past or inside the cut. Thread uses 0.61343×pitch for external and 0.54125×pitch for internal.
- **Holes:** circular inside drawings, with centre lines and the ¾ thread arc.
- **Patterns:** `grid(...)` and `radial(...)` (the radial form adds a pitch circle).
- **Other parts:** walls and partitions as thickened outlines with mitred corners (no door or window cuts), section planes, and magnifiers.
- **Stack and drawing layouts (`src/drawing.rs`):** every child sits on one datum. A nested frame centres its content, while a root frame keeps its datum and the view is just the content. A drawing's label becomes a footnote under it.
- **Units and scale:** px-per-unit = root density × unit × inherited `scale`, and widths, heights, translates, line points and max-width scale with it. Validation and the >10000 px "scale is a ratio" warning match the original.

**Shared-file edits (all small)**
- `compile.rs`/`main.rs`: a `Ctx.sk` field, plus pipeline calls: expand, then recompute the cascade if the tree grew, prepare, and size warnings after measure.
- `layout.rs`: one hook in `measure`. I also changed `measure_flow` so that a box with nothing in its flow uses its explicit width/height instead of the padding box. That is generic behaviour I verified against the original.
- `render.rs`:
  - hooks for my chrome and shapes;
  - a block with zero width or height now emits no rect;
  - bounds now respect each shape's offset under rotation;
  - a root stack or drawing starts its view from empty;
  - stylesheet slot order fixed for the drawing types;
  - `node_classes`/`inline_style` made public;
  - the old `node_matrix` is now unused (warning only).
- `scene.rs`: drawing labels become a footnote; sketch labels become text; line labels are kept on the node (plane letters).
- `types.rs`: added `breakline`, `shoulder`, `threadline`.
- `geom.rs`: arc bounds are sampled at 24 points. This changes `|path|` output too; I checked it against the original.

**Known gaps**
- **`hatch(angle, spacing, colour)` fills:** our build fails with "invalid color 'hatch'". I worked out the output format but could not reproduce the pattern-id hash.
- **Descendant selectors** such as `|hidden| |centerline|` aren't supported by the cascade (drawing_turned needs this).
- **Thread sense after a break:** when a break separates the threaded run, the original sometimes marks it internal and I couldn't find its rule.
- **Mirrored features outside drawings:** off-axis copies are decided from `translate`, not the laid-out position.
- **Generic validation** isn't done: e.g. "'draw' has no meaning on '|box|'", "'density' is scene config", "'|line|' requires 'points'".
- **Small cases:**
  - rare 4-decimal rounding ties;
  - text inside mirrored sketches widens the original's view, not ours;
  - a magnifier with `stroke: none` draws its circle 0.5 px bigger in the original.

**Notes for whoever does drawing annotations**
- **Tagged segments:** `drawing::sketch_tags(ctx, i)` returns each `:name` segment or `point():name` station in px. They are in the sketch's pen frame, which is where its group transform sits, after mirror, revolve and break; a tagged fillet is an arc carrying its radius. Raw pen output in units is `ctx.sk.base[&i]`.
- **Units:** `drawing::ps(ctx, i)` is px per unit, so a dimension value is the px length divided by ps.
- **Breaks:** `ctx.sk.laid[&i].brk` holds the cut stations and the shift in px. The true length across a break is the drawn length plus the shift.
- **Pattern copies:** `drawing::pattern_copy(ctx, wrapper, k)` (1-based) resolves things like `plate.pin.2`; the wrapper keeps the id.
- **Drawing size:** the content box is computed in `drawing::measure_frame` before the content is centred, so annotation extents need adding there. Planes are laid out after the other parts, from their extent.
- **Shared CSS:** I already add `.lini-dim-text`, `.lini-marker-dim` and the plane rules through `out.extra_rules`, and gave them slots. Use the identical rule text so they de-duplicate.
